elements.quote: Objective: We aimed to systematically identify and critically assess the clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) for the management of critically ill patients with COVID-19 with the AGREE II instrument.
elements.reason: The abstract states the study aims to systematically identify and critically assess CPGs, but it does not explicitly label the report as a “systematic review” within the abstract text provided.

elements.quote: Objective: We aimed to systematically identify and critically assess the clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) for the management of critically ill patients with COVID-19 with the AGREE II instrument.
elements.reason: A clear statement of the main objective is provided.

elements.quote: We included any guideline that provided recommendations on the management of critically ill patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: Only the inclusion criterion is explicitly stated; no explicit exclusion criteria are reported in the abstract text provided.

elements.quote: We searched Medline, CINAHL, EMBASE, CNKI, CBM, WanFang, and grey literature from November 2019 - November 2020.
elements.reason: Information sources are named, but the abstract provides a date range rather than an explicit “last searched” date for each source.
The abstract reports assessing quality with the AGREE II instrument, but it does not specify methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies.

elements.quote: We destructively summarized CPGs characteristics. We assessed the quality with the AGREE II instrument and we summarized relevant therapeutic interventions.
elements.reason: Methods for presenting/synthesizing results are described (descriptive summary of characteristics and summarizing interventions).

elements.quote: Results: We retrieved 3,907 records and 71 CPGs were included.
elements.reason: The total number included (71 CPGs) is reported, but the abstract does not report the total number of participants nor additional study/participant characteristics.

elements.quote: Means (Standard Deviations) of the scores for the 6 domains of the AGREE II instrument were 65%(SD19.56%), 39%(SD19.64%), 27%(SD19.48%), 70%(SD15.74%), 26%(SD18.49%), 42%(SD34.91) for the scope and purpose, stakeholder involvement, rigor of development, clarity of presentation, applicability, editorial independence domains, respectively. Most of the CPGs showed a low overall quality (less than 40%).
elements.reason: Results are provided (domain scores and overall quality), but they are not presented as main outcome results in the PRISMA “main outcomes” sense (e.g., no per-outcome study/participant counts).
The abstract does not indicate that a meta-analysis was conducted.
The abstract does not indicate that groups were compared with a direction of effect.
The abstract does not briefly summarize limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: Conclusion: Future CPGs for COVID-19 need to rely, for their development, on standard evidence-based methods and tools.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation/implication of the findings.
The abstract text provided does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract text provided does not report the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: A possible explanation might be the extreme conditions under which these CPGs were developed including global uncertainty about the natural history of the COVID-19 infection, the lack of direct evidence, and external pressures to produce rapid advice
elements.reason: The rationale describes important uncertainties (e.g., global uncertainty about natural history and lack of direct evidence) and the context affecting existing CPGs, but it does not clearly summarize the broader current state of knowledge beyond this point.

elements.quote: Given the extraordinary burden that the pandemic has created on the emergency and critical care units worldwide, there is an urgent need for evidence-based guidance to facilitate optimal clinical and policy decisionmaking.
elements.reason: The introduction explicitly explains the importance/need for the review by stating an urgent need for evidence-based guidance to support clinical and policy decision-making.

elements.quote: Four previous reviews have assessed the quality of COVID-19 CPGs [16-18]... However, an assessment of all the CPGs focused on the management of critically ill COVID -19 patients was lacking. We, therefore, aimed to systematically identify the CPGs for the management of critically ill patients with COVID-19, and critically assess their quality for both clinical and methodological purposes.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes existing similar reviews and then explains the gap (no assessment of all critically ill COVID-19 management CPGs), motivating the current review.

The provided evidence does not show that this review proposes and evaluates an intervention effect with a described mechanism of action; it focuses on identifying and critically assessing clinical practice guidelines.

No logic model describing hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes is presented in the retrieved evidence; the review is about appraisal/quality assessment of guidelines rather than a described complex intervention implementation model.

elements.quote: Objective: We aimed to systematically identify and critically assess the clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) for the management of critically ill patients with COVID-19 with the AGREE II instrument.

No outcome-specific risk-of-bias judgements displayed alongside study results are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No evidence in the retrieved text describes presenting, for every outcome and study, group-level summary statistics (e.g., per group within each included study).
No evidence in the retrieved text reports an effect estimate and its precision for every outcome and study.

Although a PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) and several tables are mentioned, the retrieved evidence does not show that results for outcomes are presented visually/textually with a corresponding tabular display for each study/outcome.
The retrieved evidence does not state the source of study-level data when multiple data sources were used.
The retrieved evidence does not identify results that were computed or estimated rather than directly reported for each study/outcome.

The retrieved evidence describes AGREE II quality assessment methods and some domain-level scores, but it does not report, for each synthesis, a brief summary of the relevant characteristics and risk of bias of the contributing studies.
Although the manuscript reports that 71 CPGs were included and that AGREE II assessments were performed, the retrieved evidence does not identify the studies contributing to each synthesis.
The retrieved Results text and tables describe selection/CPGs and coverage of therapeutic interventions, but do not report results of any statistical syntheses.
No meta-analysis summary estimates and precision (e.g., CI/credible interval) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No measures of statistical heterogeneity (e.g., I²/tau²) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No results from other statistical synthesis methods (with synthesized results and precision/equivalent) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not present synthesis methods that lack an effect estimate, nor any relevant statistics with interpretation.
No group comparisons are presented with an effect direction in the retrieved Results/tables.
No mean-difference syntheses are reported, so scale units, limits, direction of benefit, or minimally important difference cannot be identified in the retrieved evidence.
No re-expressed standardized mean difference syntheses (and related instrument details) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No reported investigations of possible causes of heterogeneity among study results were found in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not report subgroup analyses or identify studies contributing to each subgroup.
The retrieved evidence does not include interpretation of heterogeneity analyses with attention to observational nature or confounding.
No subgroup-analysis results (interaction-test P values, subgroup estimates, precision, or heterogeneity) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not report differences between subgroup effects and their precision.
No meta-regression results (coefficient P values and precision) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
Although images are present (figures 1 and 2), the retrieved evidence does not show any meta-regression scatterplots or label them as such.
The retrieved evidence does not describe results of informal heterogeneity investigations.
The retrieved evidence does not report results of any sensitivity analyses.
No discussion of robustness of the main analysis in light of sensitivity analyses is provided in the retrieved evidence.
No tables comparing original and sensitivity-analysis results, assumptions, and contributing studies are found in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not contain sensitivity-analysis forest plots.
The retrieved evidence does not report any risk-of-bias assessments due to missing results (arising from reporting biases) for each synthesis.
No information is provided in the retrieved evidence about use of a tool for assessing risk of bias due to missing results, including item responses, judgements, and supporting information.
The retrieved evidence contains no funnel plots and no reporting of funnel-plot components (effect estimate, precision measure, contour milestones).
The retrieved evidence does not mention any funnel-plot asymmetry test or report an exact P value/statistics.
No sensitivity analyses examining missing results are reported in the retrieved evidence or compared with a primary analysis.
The retrieved evidence does not include any study-by-synthesis matrix for selective non-reporting assessments.
The retrieved evidence does not report studies with missing results displayed beneath forest plots or in a table.
The retrieved evidence does not report an overall certainty/confidence level for every important outcome.
The retrieved evidence provides no reasons for rating certainty down or up.
The retrieved evidence does not show certainty communicated alongside results/outcomes using any section-appropriate format.
The retrieved evidence does not mention evidence summary tables (e.g., GRADE Summary of Findings tables).

elements.quote: In the review by Kowalski et al., for instance, 46 rapid guidelines developed by WHO and NICE were assessed and obtained average scores of 71% and 81% in the rigor of development domain [10] .
elements.reason: The discussion places the study’s findings in context by comparing them to results from another review (Kowalski et al.) regarding the rigor of development scores of rapid guidelines.

elements.quote: Almost half of the CPGs were of poor methodological quality, and only 3, were of acceptable quality to recommend their use [ 26 , 35 , 84 ].
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly states limitations in the included evidence by reporting poor methodological quality for many included clinical practice guidelines.

elements.quote: Despite using only 2 appraisers meets the minimum standard for AGREE II, it potentially may reduce the reliability of results and increases the likelihood that betweenrater variability may directly affect the results.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly discusses a limitation of the review process (using only 2 appraisers for AGREE II) and links it to reliability/variability concerns.

elements.quote: Moreover, the continuously evolving evidence landscape of COVID-19 would require an ongoing process of monitoring and updating as some recommendations are likely to change [96]. ... However, this study is not free of limitations. We had to exclude, for now, CPGs that were written in languages that were not covered by our research team (i.e., Japanese). Moreover, the assessments were conducted only on CPGs that were either published in peer review journals or posted in official websites as CPG full documents, without considering unpublished or supplementary material, therefore, it is possible that some information was missing to inform the quality of the CPGs in this iteration but it is planned to be covered in the following series of this living review.
elements.reason: The impact is described for some process limitations (e.g., excluding languages and unpublished/supplementary material could mean some information was missing for quality assessment). However, the evidence also includes other limitations (e.g., reviewer/appraiser considerations) where the potential impacts are not consistently tied to each limitation within the retrieved discussion text.

elements.quote: Our results will be helpful for healthcare professionals, CPG developers, CPG users/implementers, and decisionmakers. Intensive care clinicians now have a summary of the available CPG and can choose among them the most trustworthy to follow.
elements.reason: The Discussion explains implications for practice by stating how healthcare professionals/clinicians can use the findings to choose trustworthy CPGs and implement guidance.

elements.quote: Developers and decision-makers can also choose from our list the CPGs that are of higher quality to eventually adapt or endorse a CPG to be used in their contexts.
elements.reason: Implications are described for decision-makers (e.g., adoption/endorsement), but the evidence does not explicitly discuss implications for policy (e.g., policy-makers, guideline policy-making, or governmental/regulatory policy).

elements.quote: However, we acknowledge that further methodological research is needed to provide better guidance on RGs development.
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies a need for further methodological research, but it does not provide explicit, actionable recommendations for future research beyond this statement.

elements.quote: The larger study was registered in the PROSPERO register ( https:// www.crd.york.ac.uk/ prospero/ display _ record. php?ID=CRD42020179872) [21] Our review was registered as a traditional systematic review of CPGs but given the rapid evolution of the pandemic and the speed of the evidence synthesis, we thought that a living review would have been more appropriate and useful for decision-makers and CPGs users and implementers.
elements.reason: Registration is mentioned, but the review’s register name and registration number are not explicitly provided; only the larger study’s PROSPERO registration (CRD42020179872) is reported.

elements.quote: The larger study was registered in the PROSPERO register ( https:// www.crd.york.ac.uk/ prospero/ display _ record. php?ID=CRD42020179872) [21]
elements.reason: A registration link in PROSPERO is provided for the larger study, but the evidence does not explicitly state where the specific review protocol can be accessed or that no protocol was prepared.
No amendments to registration or protocol information are described in the retrieved evidence.
No reasons for any amendments to registration or protocol information are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No stage of the review at which any amendments were implemented is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: This work was supported by the Research Chair for Evidence-Based Health Care and Knowledge Translation, Deanship of Scientific Research, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
elements.reason: The review’s non-financial/financial support source is described; however, no grant identifier is provided.

elements.quote: The funding source had no role or influence in the study design, data collection, data analysis and publication decision.
elements.reason: The role (lack of involvement) of the funding source in key review stages is explicitly stated.
No declaration is provided in the retrieved evidence about review authors’ competing interests or author relationships/activities that could be relevant to or influence the review.
The retrieved evidence does not report whether competing interests existed, nor how any competing interests were managed in the review processes.

elements.reason: The manuscript reports that supplementary material is available online, but it does not explicitly state the public availability of template data collection forms, extracted data, analysis data, analytic code, or other specific review materials.
